feed.name: jordyn-first-car
feed.purpose: Current used-car inventory for the family: a safety/TCO view for Jordyn and a premium-EV depreciation view for Kate.

budget.note: $15k is Jordyn's preferred target. Kate's EV band normally stops at $25k; only explicitly named interests may extend to $30k, with stricter model-specific ceilings where applicable. A named model with fewer than three qualifying PNW examples receives national fallback inventory costed with $2,000 shipping.

nationalFallback.trigger: Fewer than 3 qualifying listings in the 250-mile PNW search

feed.discovery: Broad inventory is Bellevue-centered within 250 miles, with no model whitelist or safety filter at query time. Only explicitly named Kate models with fewer than three qualifying PNW examples are supplemented nationally; those cars are tagged national-fallback and carry $2,000 shipping.
feed.refresh: Regenerated nightly from live Autotrader inventory. Listings appear and sell quickly — always confirm against sourceUrl before acting.
howToReadThis: null means UNKNOWN and is always distinct from false. Never render a null as a negative.
Powertrain is resolved from the VIN via NHTSA vPIC, never from the model name. Check powertrain.vinVerified before trusting electricRangeMi or energy costs.
Safety equipment carries a confidence level. "vin-trim-confirmed" is manufacturer-reported for that trim; "model-year-typical" is research, not a fact about this car.
reliability lives in reliabilityByModelYear, keyed by listing.reliabilityKey. It is model-year scope and says nothing about the condition of the individual car.
vehicleHistory badges are affirming/negating pairs; null means not reported, NOT the negative.
Start from shortlists.topOverall and shortlists.topElectric — the full listings array is long.
Bargain score is separate from TCO and uses the published 25/20/15/15/10/10/5 component weights. Read its riskGate before treating a depreciated car as actionable.
Only listings returned by the current successful scan are published. Cars that disappear are retained in the Vault Listing History, not in this feed.
listings[] holds full detail for the shortlisted cars. Every car the sweep found is in the companion file jordyn-all.json (see allCars.url) — use it for market-wide questions.

marketAnalysis is where the population-level answers live: cohorts (model + generation + powertrain + battery, NOT model name), a safety-gated primary ranking, opportunities found from the data, and the methodology needed to challenge any of it.
Safety is a GATE, not a weight. marketAnalysis.safetyFirst excludes a car only when AEB is CONFIRMED ABSENT — never when it is merely unverified.

jordynPicks is what SHE chose, scored with the same model as everything else. It is never a filter on the rankings. Read entries[].delta against jordynPicks.baseline, and weight `stated` picks above `thumbed` ones.
bands is the curated view: start there rather than with listings[] or allCars. bands.kate is BATTERY-ELECTRIC ONLY by rule — the absence of petrol cars there is deliberate, not a gap in the data.

ODOMETER vs ANNUAL MILEAGE: the Highlander's odometer is 135,000 (highlanderAndPlans.highlander.odometerMiles). Every field ending in MilesPerYear is annual driving — 17,000 is what Kate drives in a year, NOT a mileage reading.
All money is US dollars, whole units. All distances are miles.
feed.privacy: Unlisted capability URL. Not encrypted — treat the URL itself as the secret.

fieldNotes.fleetStrategies: Whole-fleet options compared on present value at 5%/yr, at both a 2-year and a 6-year horizon. Scenario A is the reference (Kate keeps the Highlander, Jordyn gets a cheap EV); every Scenario B swaps that round. Each Scenario B candidate is costed at KATE's 13,520 mi/yr and the Highlander moves to Jordyn's 6,760 — comparing them on one driver's mileage would be meaningless.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.*.cashRequiredNowUsd: Actual money out the door at t=0. Deliberately EXCLUDES the retained Highlander's value, which is an economic opportunity cost rather than a cash outflow. Never substitute this for npvUsd or nominalTcoUsd — an $11k car for Jordyn needs far less cash today than a $23k EV for Kate even where six-year totals converge.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.*.nominalTcoUsd: Undiscounted total economic cost over the horizon, including the retained-asset opportunity cost. Identity is published on scenario.audit and reproduces exactly from the component values.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.*.npvUsd: Present value of that same stream at 5%. Purchase and sales tax at t=0 undiscounted, operating costs discounted in the year incurred, terminal value discounted back from the end of the horizon.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.horizons.*.breakEvenNpvU: The NPV a Scenario B must come in at or below to be financially equal to Scenario A. It IS Scenario A's own NPV — there is no separate hurdle.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.*.breakEvenPurchasePrice: Purchase price at which this model's scenario NPV equals Scenario A's, solved NUMERICALLY by recosting the car at trial prices. $1 of price does NOT move NPV by $1 — sales tax adds to it and a dearer car returns more residual, which is discounted back and partly offsets. sensitivityPerDollar publishes the actual figure (observed ~0.86–0.92), so the correction is visible rather than assumed away. A null priceUsd with a `reason` means no price in the search range breaks even; that is a real answer, not a failure.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.highlander.effectiveMpg: EPA/catalog 22 mpg × 0.85 local duty-cycle factor = 18.7 mpg, corroborated independently by 18.6 mpg observed over 46,000 miles. Applied ONCE, inside the shared cost model; it is not re-applied by any consumer.
fieldNotes.fleetStrategies.highlander.opportunityCo: Retaining the Highlander carries its realisable value as a t=0 cost and credits its residual back at the horizon. The `valueConsumed` line on its own TCO expresses the same economics as depreciation — the two are alternatives, never additive.
fieldNotes.listing.priceStatus: "as-listed" = the scraped asking price stands. "disputed" = the SELLER has told us the listed price is wrong — do NOT use askingPriceUsd as a real price, and do not present it as one. Read priceDispute.dealerSaysUsd for what they actually said and sixYearTcoRangeUsd for the cost implication. "confirmed" = verified by phone, askingPriceUsd is correct.
fieldNotes.listing.priceDispute: A hand-verified correction from a phone call, not a scrape. Survives the nightly refresh. Where present it OVERRIDES the listing. The car is deliberately kept on the list — a wrong price is a reason to re-cost it, not to discard it.
fieldNotes.listing.sixYearTcoRangeUsd: Present only for disputed prices: the six-year cost computed across the range the seller gave, rather than a single figure implying precision we do not have. costToOwn elsewhere is computed at rankedAtPriceUsd, the midpoint of that range.
fieldNotes.listing.powertrain: Resolved from the VIN via NHTSA vPIC, never from the model name — a "Hyundai Ioniq" is sold as a hybrid, a plug-in hybrid AND a battery EV. `vinVerified: false` means range/energy/battery figures are model-level assumptions; a `caution` string is then present.
fieldNotes.listing.electricDriveShare: Fraction of miles actually driven on electricity at 130 mi/week (~19 mi/day). 1 = battery-electric. A plug-in hybrid with ~50 miles of range approaches 1 at this duty cycle, i.e. it runs as a de-facto EV; a short-range plug-in does not. This is the meaningful measure of "primarily electric drive", not battery presence.
fieldNotes.listing.safety.*.confidence: "vin-trim-confirmed" = the manufacturer reports this as standard for this VIN's trim (NHTSA vPIC). "model-year-typical" = model-year research, NOT confirmed for this car. "unknown" = no data. vPIC is a paperwork record, not a physical inspection — confirm on the vehicle.
fieldNotes.listing.safety.*.equipped: true only when confirmed standard. null means unconfirmed, which is NOT the same as absent — many manufacturers simply do not submit this field (Toyota reports blind-spot for 0 of its listings here).
fieldNotes.listing.safety.iihsAward: IIHS does not test every powertrain variant of a model. An award applies to the variant named in it, which may differ from this car; iihsNotRatedNote flags that case.
fieldNotes.listing.battery.riskFactor: 0 = no modelled degradation/replacement exposure; higher = more. Feeds the batteryAllowance line in costToOwn.
fieldNotes.listing.battery.federalWarranty: US federal minimum is 8 years / 100,000 miles on the traction battery, transferable to subsequent owners. Some states and manufacturers exceed it.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.band: clean | ok | watch | concern | unknown — a qualitative band, NOT a numeric score. Scope is the model-year, so it says nothing about the condition of an individual car. Get a pre-purchase inspection. `unknown` with recordRetrieved:false means the NHTSA lookup found no matching model — ABSENCE OF DATA, never a clean record.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.queriedAsNhtsaM: The model name actually queried. NHTSA matches names exactly and splits many models by powertrain variant ("IONIQ HYBRID" vs "IONIQ PLUG-IN HYBRID" vs "IONIQ ELECTRIC"; "CLARITY PLUG-IN HYBRID" vs "CLARITY FUEL CELL"), returning an empty result with HTTP 200 on a miss. The variant is chosen from the VIN-resolved powertrain, never by name similarity. This field lets you verify we asked about the right car.
fieldNotes.reliabilityByModelYear.*.sourceUrl: Triangulated from freely accessible public sources, primarily NHTSA complaints/recalls. NOT J.D. Power and NOT Consumer Reports. Complaint counts are not adjusted for sales volume, so raw counts are not comparable between a high-volume and a low-volume model.
fieldNotes.listing.vehicleHistory: From the dealer-supplied CARFAX/AutoCheck summary on the listing. Badges come in affirming/negating pairs, so true AND false are both affirmative statements from the report; null means NEITHER badge was present, i.e. NOT REPORTED. Never read null as the negative. Always pull a full VIN history before buying.
fieldNotes.listing.costToOwn: totalCostOfOwnership = purchasePrice + shipping + salesTax + fuelAndElectricity + maintenance + insurance + registrationAndFees + majorRepairReserve − resaleValueRecovered. National fallback cars carry a $2,000 shipping estimate; local PNW cars carry $0. Inputs are in costAssumptions. ⚠️ ALWAYS read costedFor and milesPerYear before quoting a total.
fieldNotes.listing.inventoryScope: `pnw` means the normal Bellevue-centered 250-mile search. `national-fallback` appears only for a model explicitly named by Kate when fewer than three qualifying local examples exist; shippingEstimateUsd is then included in TCO, NPV and cash-required calculations.
fieldNotes.listing.costToOwnByDriver: The SAME car costed both ways, so the assignment question ("who should drive this?") can be answered directly. Kate drives exactly double Jordyn (13,520 vs 6,760 mi/yr), so an efficient car saves twice as much parked under her — that ratio is the whole reason the question has an answer. `estimated: true` on the kate block means only the Jordyn-mileage figure existed and was reused; treat it as a floor, not a computed total.
fieldNotes.listing.costToOwn.*.netPresentValueUsd: The same cost stream discounted to today at 5%/yr (costAssumptions.npvDiscountRatePctPerYear). Purchase + sales tax are undiscounted; recurring costs are spread evenly across the years and discounted annually; the resale credit is discounted back from the end of the window. It runs a little BELOW totalCostOfOwnership because costs that land late are weighted down — it shows DIRECTION, not added precision. Present on every cost block, so costToOwnByDriver carries it for BOTH Jordyn and Kate, and it matches the NPV shown on the page.
fieldNotes.listing.costToOwn.*.insurance: This car's own premium ONLY. The $2,400/yr to add Jordyn as a driver is a household cost — owed whichever car is bought — and is counted once in highlanderAndPlans, never here. Do not add it to a listing.
fieldNotes.listing.repairOutlook: ONE framework applied to every powertrain. Each hazard attaches only to components that powertrain actually has — an EV carries no engine, transmission, exhaust or emissions hazard; a plug-in hybrid carries BOTH the engine set and the high-voltage set. expectedReserveUsd is Σ(probability × cost) and is the budget number, already included in costToOwn.*.costs.majorRepairReserve; worstCaseExposure is the single largest plausible bill and is deliberately NOT averaged into it. Probabilities are engineering estimates scaled by age, odometer and ownership length, with stated ranges — not actuarial data. See repairHazardCatalog for each hazard's cost range and basis. NOTE: an earlier version of this model charged electric cars a battery allowance and charged gasoline and hybrid cars nothing for major repairs, which biased every cost comparison against EVs; correcting it moved electric cars up roughly 24 ranking places on average.
fieldNotes.listing.batteryHealth: Capacity loss ONLY. It reduces range and resale value and is deliberately NOT charged as a repair; catastrophic pack failure is a separate hazard in repairOutlook. Projected from pack age, odometer and thermal-management type for Seattle's mild climate and mostly overnight AC home charging — the two conditions that most slow degradation. Heat and frequent DC fast charging are the main accelerators and neither is expected here. This is a projection, not a measurement: verify with a real state-of-health readout (LeafSpy or equivalent) before buying.
fieldNotes.listing.viability2032: Coarse judgement of whether the car is still economically worth owning at the end of the 6-year window, from age, mileage, projected battery health, and the size of the expected repair reserve relative to the car's value. Condition of the individual car dominates all of it — get a pre-purchase inspection.
fieldNotes.repairHazardCatalog: Definitions for the hazard ids referenced by listing.repairOutlook.components, stated once here rather than repeated on every car. Includes the cost range and the basis for each probability.
fieldNotes.listing.ranking.matchScore: Internal 0-100 fit score used to order the page: safety, then cost to own, then longevity, multiplied by reliability and title-history factors. Powertrain-neutral by design — electric cars are not given a bonus, so where they win they win on cost. Not a quality rating.
fieldNotes.listing.stillListed: Always true in this current-inventory feed. Listings absent from the latest successful scan are removed here and retained only in the Vault Listing History.
fieldNotes.listing.bargain: A separate 0-100 depreciation-value score: 25% discount from original MSRP, 20% reliability/catastrophic-failure risk, 15% local manufacturer serviceability, 15% driving character/performance, 10% premium interior/features, 10% range/charging suitability and 5% rarity/interestingness. It does not replace TCO, and an open risk gate remains visible.
fieldNotes.listing.kateResearch: Model-specific buying criteria and required checks for Kate. Jaguar I-PACE entries include every potentially applicable HV-battery campaign for the model year plus the latest Jaguar VIN lookup status; absence from the open-recall result is not represented as proof of completion.

shortlists.note: Two rankings on purpose. topOverall is powertrain-neutral. topElectric applies the stated preference for primarily-electric driving, kept as a separate list so the bias is visible rather than hidden inside matchScore.

topOverall.name: 2022 MAZDA MX-30 Electric w/ Premium Plus Pkg

topElectric.note: Battery-electric and plug-in hybrids only, VIN-verified, ranked by overall fit — NOT by electric share. Ranking by share alone would put every 100%-electric BEV above every plug-in and hide the fact that a 53-mile Volt covers ~85% of these miles on electricity while costing several thousand less to own. Read electricDriveShare alongside the rank.

bands.note: Two candidate sets with different rules. Jordyn: $10-15k, any powertrain, decided on safety then cost to own. Kate: $15-25k for battery-electric cars, extended to model-specific ceilings no higher than $30k only for named interests, decided on fit, risk and depreciation value.
bands.cohortNote: Cohorts are model + generation + battery, NOT model name. A 2013 Leaf and a 2023 Leaf share a badge and nothing else, so a range built on the name alone would average incomparable cars.
bands.exemplarNote: Two per cohort: the best of the group by overall fit, and the cheapest to own that still clears the safety floor. Deliberately not the two cheapest, which surfaces the worst-condition examples and makes every group look like a bargain it is not.

openRecalls.remedy: This is a placeholder campaign for the permanent remedy, which is stillunder development. This information will be updated when this activity is completed.

As an interim repair, the vehicles will have software installed to restrict the maximum state of charge to 90% whilst a permanent remedy is developed.

In line with recommendations made by manufacturers whohave had similar issues and until such time as the interim remedy has been completed, JLR request that customers take the following precautionsto minimise the thermal overload which can lead to vehicle fire:

• Only charge their vehicle to a maximum of 90% state of charge
•Park away from structures
• Charge outside

Customers can monitor the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App or inside the vehicle and should seek to physically stop the charging by unplugging the cable before a 90% state of charge is exceeded.

There will be no charge to the owners for this interim repair.

At your visit, your preferred Jaguar retailer/authorized repairer willprovide an update to the Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) software that will monitor the High Voltage (HV) battery operational status. Thiswill provide indication in the event the HV battery exhibits conditionswhich may lead to thermal overload condition.This software provides anenhanced level of driver warnings in relation to HV battery condition and in the event the software determines a risk exists, the HV battery charging capacity is limited to up to 75%.If this happens, the vehicle will prompt you to visit a Jaguar retailer/authorized repairer. Your retailer will inspect, and if necessary replace the affected HV battery module/assembly at no cost to you.Some vehicles also provide a Charging Limit feature that can be used by customers to limit the charge level. Customers may, until the recall is completed, set the charge limit to 75%.Instructions of how to limit the charging limit can be found in the Jaguar I-PACE Owner’s Manual in the Vehicle Preconditioning – Charging Limits section at www.ownerinfo.jaguar.com.Customers can also monitor and control the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App and stop charging when it reaches 75% state of charge.There will be no charge to the owners for this repair.

fleetStrategies.method: Purchase price and sales tax fall at t=0 undiscounted; operating costs are spread evenly and discounted in the year incurred; terminal value is discounted back from the end of the horizon. Retaining the Highlander carries its realisable value as a t=0 opportunity cost, credited back as residual at the horizon — an economic cost, not a cash outflow, so it is in NPV and nominal but NOT in cash-required-now.

highlander.label: 2017 Toyota Highlander Limited
highlander.mpgBasis: EPA/catalog 22 mpg × 0.85 local duty-cycle factor = 18.7 mpg, independently corroborated by 18.6 mpg observed over 46,000 miles. Applied ONCE — the factor lives in ASSUMPTIONS.dutyCycle and is not re-applied downstream.
highlander.opportunityCostNote: Counted once, as a t=0 opportunity cost in any scenario that retains the car. The `valueConsumed` line on its TCO expresses the same economics as depreciation and is deliberately NOT added on top.

household.teenDriverAdditionBasis: Agent quote, $200/mo, to add Jordyn as a third driver. Owed under every scenario, so it shifts no ranking — but the totals would be wrong without it.

audit.identity: nominalTcoUsd = Σ vehicles.upfrontUsd + Σ vehicles.recurringUsd + household.teenDriverAdditionUsd − Σ vehicles.terminalValueUsd

2.breakEvenNote: Any Scenario B whose 2-year NPV comes in at or below $32,566 is financially equal to or better than keeping the Highlander with Kate. That threshold is just Scenario A's own NPV — there is nothing else to clear.

fleetStrategies.cashVsEconomic: cashRequiredNowUsd, nominalTcoUsd and npvUsd are three different things and are never interchangeable. Buying Jordyn an $11k car needs far less cash today than buying Kate a $23k EV even where six-year totals land close — that gap is the whole reason the two-year view exists.
fleetStrategies.optionality: The two-year figures deliberately do NOT assume the Highlander is sold at year 2. Its year-2 residual is reported on the same basis as any other terminal value, so buying Kate an EV now and revisiting the Highlander later can be evaluated without re-deriving anything.

highlanderAndPlans.note: The Highlander is ALREADY OWNED. odometerMiles is its actual mileage; milesPerYear figures are annual driving. Do not confuse the two.

highlander.worthToKeepBasis: Median dealer asking price for 32 comparable 2016-18 Highlanders at 110-165k miles within 250 miles of 98006, Autotrader 2026-09-04. Context only — not realisable without a private sale.
highlander.tradeInBasis: VERIFIED — KBB trade-in value for this VIN, Good condition, ZIP 98006, 2026-09-04. Range $14,810–$17,110.
highlander.tradeInTaxCreditBasis: RCW 82.08.010(1)(a)(i) excludes separately stated like-kind trade-in from taxable selling price. At 10.8% that is $1,724 on a $15,960 trade.
highlander.tradeInFrictionNote: Trading destroys about $5,040 of value (what it is worth to keep, less what a dealer gives), of which Washington's trade-in sales-tax credit returns $1,724. Net friction ≈ $3,316.
highlander.note: Running cost only — fuel, maintenance, tabs and the expected major-repair reserve. It excludes the teen-driver insurance addition, which the household pays because Jordyn starts driving at all, not because she drives this particular car.

risk.source: NHTSA complaintsByVehicle, MY2017 Toyota Highlander, queried 2026-09-04

hazards.label: UA80 8-speed transmission failure
hazards.note: First model year of the UA80. Multiple owners report the replacement transmission is backordered with no US supply — so the risk is not only the bill but the car being off the road for months.

hazards.label: 2GR-FKS timing-cover oil leak (FIPG sealant at the T junction)
hazards.note: Requires full engine removal. Documented across Toyota/Lexus V6 applications 2014–2019.

risk.verdict: The premise that this is a low-risk known quantity does not survive the complaint file. It is a first-year powertrain with a documented five-figure failure mode and a parts-supply problem.

highlander.odometerMilesNote: ACTUAL ODOMETER READING, not annual mileage.
highlander.mpgBasis: EPA combined rating (the catalogue sticker). NOT the figure fuel is costed at — see effectiveMpgUsedInCosting.
highlander.effectiveMpgBasis: Every tcoUsd and energy figure in this block is ALREADY costed at 18.7 mpg — the EPA 22 × 85% observed duty-cycle (costAssumptions.dutyCycle), matching JC's measured 18.6 mpg. Do NOT also lower mpg to 18.6: the duty-cycle factor already applies the real-world penalty, so changing the sticker would double-count it and overstate the Highlander's cost.

suspension-brakes.basis: Engineering estimate. Struts, bushings, wheel bearings and calipers on a decade-old car. Regenerative braking meaningfully extends pad and rotor life on hybrids and EVs, so the low end of the range applies to them.

ev-drive-unit.component: Drive unit, inverter or onboard charger
ev-drive-unit.basis: Engineering estimate. The electric drivetrain has one moving part and an excellent field record; the money risk sits in power electronics and the onboard charger rather than the motor.

ev-battery-failure.basis: Recurrent Auto's fleet analysis puts out-of-warranty battery REPLACEMENT at roughly 1.5% of all EVs, and well under 1% for 2016-and-newer model years, once recall campaigns are excluded. Widened here to account for out-of-warranty repair on cheap older cars and for the fact that a used or refurbished pack — not a $16,000 dealer pack — is the realistic remedy at this price point. This is FAILURE ONLY; gradual capacity loss is handled in batteryHealth().

hv-thermal-hvac.basis: Engineering estimate. Electric compressors and coolant heaters are a known EV maintenance item. Passively-cooled packs skip this hardware entirely, which is why they are cheaper to fix and worse at surviving heat.

transmission.basis: Engineering estimate. The single most expensive common failure on a high-mileage conventional automatic or CVT. Deliberately NOT applied to hybrids: Toyota/Hyundai/Kia hybrids use a planetary eCVT with no clutch packs or torque converter, which is a genuinely different and more durable device.

cooling-fuel.basis: Engineering estimate. Water pumps, radiators, thermostats, fuel pumps, coil packs — individually modest, collectively near-certain across six years on a car of this age.

emissions.basis: Engineering estimate, informed by the high rate of P0420-type emissions faults on 10+ year old cars and by catalytic-converter theft rates in the Puget Sound region. Required to pass Washington emissions and to sell the car.

engine.basis: Engineering estimate. Catastrophic engine failure is uncommon on the Japanese/Korean 4-cylinders in this roster; the risk is concentrated in neglected examples, which is why a service history matters more than the average.

starter-alternator.basis: Engineering estimate. Full hybrids and EVs have neither component — hybrids start the engine with the traction motor and charge the 12 V system from the high-voltage pack.

hybrid-battery.basis: Engineering estimate. Full-hybrid packs are small and a healthy aftermarket exists, so this is a real but bounded bill rather than a write-off. Rises steeply past ~150,000 miles.

allCars.note: Every car found by the nightly sweep, not just those published to the page. Slim records: the full repair, reliability and battery detail for shortlisted cars lives in listings[]. It contains current-scan inventory only; unavailable historical listings stay in the Vault. Fields are flat: aeb/bsm rather than a nested safety object, and tco2/tco6 are plain dollar totals rather than breakdowns.

summary.note: The preferred budget is $15k; the search runs to the ceiling so cost-to-own can argue for a dearer car rather than a rule excluding it.

cohorts.note: Grouped by model + generation + powertrain + battery, NOT by model name. Averaging a 24 kWh Leaf with a 40 kWh Leaf, or an Ioniq Hybrid with an Ioniq Electric, produces a median that describes neither car.
cohorts.singletonNote: Cohorts represented by a single listing are counted below but omitted from `all` — one car is an anecdote, and carrying ~70 of them made this document large enough that clients began truncating it.

jordynAppeal.what: Upscale badges and compact SUVs that clear the safety floor and are not economically ridiculous — the cars closest to what Jordyn actually picked.

tasteProfile.basis: Weighted across 16 picks: 9 she asked for unprompted (full weight) and 7 thumbed from the earlier short list (0.4 weight, because that menu chose most of it for her).

jordynAppeal.ranking: Ranked on a blend of how closely each matches her demonstrated taste (55%) and how far below the market median it sits on six-year cost (45%). Safety is a gate applied before ranking, not a weight inside it.
jordynAppeal.premiumMeaning: Median six-year cost of these versus the whole market. A positive number is what choosing something she likes costs.

baselineComparison.note: premiumLadder bands are premiums over the BASELINE'S SIX-YEAR COST, not over its purchase price — a dearer car can be cheaper to live with. Every car in the ladder clears the safety floor and has a clean title, so the premium buys taste rather than safety.
baselineComparison.caveat: Teen insurance is an estimate pending real quotes and is the largest single line item. Treat the deltas as far more reliable than the absolute totals.

methodology.costModel: totalCostOfOwnership = purchase + shipping + salesTax + fuel/electricity + maintenance + insurance + registration + majorRepairReserve − resaleValueRecovered.

assumptions.insuranceTeenAdditionSource: Agent via JC 2026-09-01: +$200/mo to add Jordyn to a two-car policy.
assumptions.salesTaxBasis: Bellevue 98006: 10.3% combined general rate (DOR address lookup, 2026-09-04) + 0.5% additional motor-vehicle tax (RCW 82.08.020(3), raised from 0.3% on 2026-01-01).

dutyCycle.basis: Highlander measured 18.6 mpg over 46,000 mi = 84.5% of its 22 mpg EPA combined rating (JC, 2026-09-05).

repairHazards.label: Major engine repair or replacement
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Catastrophic engine failure is uncommon on the Japanese/Korean 4-cylinders in this roster; the risk is concentrated in neglected examples, which is why a service history matters more than the average.

repairHazards.label: Automatic transmission failure
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. The single most expensive common failure on a high-mileage conventional automatic or CVT. Deliberately NOT applied to hybrids: Toyota/Hyundai/Kia hybrids use a planetary eCVT with no clutch packs or torque converter, which is a genuinely different and more durable device.

repairHazards.label: Catalytic converter / emissions system
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate, informed by the high rate of P0420-type emissions faults on 10+ year old cars and by catalytic-converter theft rates in the Puget Sound region. Required to pass Washington emissions and to sell the car.

repairHazards.label: Cooling, fuel or ignition system
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Water pumps, radiators, thermostats, fuel pumps, coil packs — individually modest, collectively near-certain across six years on a car of this age.

repairHazards.label: Starter or alternator
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Full hybrids and EVs have neither component — hybrids start the engine with the traction motor and charge the 12 V system from the high-voltage pack.

repairHazards.label: Hybrid traction battery failure
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Full-hybrid packs are small and a healthy aftermarket exists, so this is a real but bounded bill rather than a write-off. Rises steeply past ~150,000 miles.

repairHazards.label: Traction battery catastrophic failure (not degradation)
repairHazards.basis: Recurrent Auto's fleet analysis puts out-of-warranty battery REPLACEMENT at roughly 1.5% of all EVs, and well under 1% for 2016-and-newer model years, once recall campaigns are excluded. Widened here to account for out-of-warranty repair on cheap older cars and for the fact that a used or refurbished pack — not a $16,000 dealer pack — is the realistic remedy at this price point. This is FAILURE ONLY; gradual capacity loss is handled in batteryHealth().

repairHazards.label: Drive unit, inverter or onboard charger
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. The electric drivetrain has one moving part and an excellent field record; the money risk sits in power electronics and the onboard charger rather than the motor.

repairHazards.label: Battery thermal management / electric HVAC
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Electric compressors and coolant heaters are a known EV maintenance item. Passively-cooled packs skip this hardware entirely, which is why they are cheaper to fix and worse at surviving heat.

repairHazards.label: Suspension, steering or brake overhaul
repairHazards.basis: Engineering estimate. Struts, bushings, wheel bearings and calipers on a decade-old car. Regenerative braking meaningfully extends pad and rotor life on hybrids and EVs, so the low end of the range applies to them.

methodology.brandIndexRationale: Scales what a repair COSTS in parts and labour, never how often it happens. It is not a "luxury penalty": hazards attach by powertrain, so a BMW i3 carries no engine, transmission, exhaust or emissions hazard at all while an X5 40e carries those plus the high-voltage set. The two are therefore modelled very differently despite sharing a badge. Indexed against published brand-average repair costs, which blend frequency and severity — applying them to cost alone is the conservative reading.
knownWeaknesses: Teen insurance is the largest single line and is an estimate, not a quote. It affects all cars similarly, so comparisons hold up better than absolute totals.

Repair probabilities are engineering estimates with stated ranges, not actuarial data. Tail risk on complex older luxury drivetrains is the most likely place for this model to be optimistic — the per-component breakdown is exposed so it can be challenged.
NHTSA complaint counts are not adjusted for sales volume and cannot be compared across models of different popularity.
Washington's used-EV sales-tax exemption appears to have lapsed and is deliberately not modelled.
methodology.howToChallenge: Every cohort exposes medianRepairReserve and its exemplars expose per-listing majorRepairReserve; repairHazardCatalog gives the probability and cost range behind each component. If an older luxury car looks cheap, check its repairOutlook components against what those repairs actually cost.

costAssumptions.note: These are the INPUTS to every costToOwn figure. Change one and every total moves.
costAssumptions.milesPerYearNote: ANNUAL driving distances. The Highlander's ODOMETER (135,000) is a separate field on highlanderAndPlans.highlander.odometerMiles — do not read an annual figure as a mileage reading.
costAssumptions.npvDiscountRateBasis: The rate behind every costToOwn.*.netPresentValueUsd. A plain round 5%/yr to show DIRECTION — later dollars count for less — NOT fitted to this household's actual cost of capital.
costAssumptions.premiumGasolineNote: Charged only to engines that specify premium (mainly the German and British cars). Roughly 12% over regular on the Eastside.

electricity.note: PSE Schedule 7 is TIERED at 600 kWh/month. This is the Tier-2 MARGINAL all-in rate — the cost of the next kWh — NOT the blended average. A Level 2 charger adds roughly 250-350 kWh/month, which pushes essentially any household into Tier 2. The fixed $7.49/month basic charge is deliberately EXCLUDED: it is paid whether or not the family owns an EV, so charging it to the car would overstate every electric option.
electricity.anchor: Verified $0.206882/kWh Tier-2 all-in, PSE "Summary of Total Current Prices - Electric" effective 2026-05-01. https://www.pse.com/en/pages/rates/schedule-summaries
electricity.forwardCurve: PSE filed a three-year rate plan on 2026-02-27 (UTC dockets 260005 electric / 260006 gas) requesting Schedule 7 increases of +16.75% (2027), +3.76% (2028), +8.81% (2029), effective early 2027. https://www.pse.com/en/pages/rates/pending-utc-filings/2026-general-rate-case
electricity.scenario: Midpoint of the as-filed request and a conservative case where the UTC approves roughly two-thirds of it, with 3-4%/yr thereafter. The UTC rarely grants a filing in full, so taking it at face value would overstate; assuming a small approval would understate.
electricity.historicalContext: PSE's all-in residential rate went from ~$0.102/kWh (Jul 2020) to $0.2017/kWh (May 2026) — a 12.4%/yr CAGR, most of it after Jan 2024. The 3-4%/yr assumed beyond 2029 is well BELOW that, so the risk on these figures is skewed toward being too low.
electricity.extrapolationWarning: 2030-2032 is extrapolation. No filed rate case covers those years.
electricity.upsideNotModelled: PSE Schedule 327 super-off-peak (12am-7am) is about $0.1214/kWh all-in and would nearly halve charging cost, but enrolment is capped at 2,500 accounts statewide so it is not the base case.

washingtonRegistration.note: Bellevue is inside the Sound Transit RTA district, so annual tabs are partly VALUE-BASED, not flat. Total = base/weight fees + RTA MVET + any EV surcharge.
washingtonRegistration.rtaMvetBasis: Assessed on 85% of ORIGINAL MSRP depreciated by the 1990 statutory schedule (RCW 81.104.160(1)(c)), NOT on the price actually paid. A cheap used car with a high original MSRP therefore still owes real money.
washingtonRegistration.evSurchargeNote: Plug-in hybrids below the range threshold owe nothing extra — e.g. a 19-mile Ford C-MAX Energi pays no EV surcharge.
washingtonRegistration.weakestInput: Original MSRP is ESTIMATED per model-year, not looked up per VIN. It is the weakest input in the registration line; each listing carries its own uncertainty string.

costAssumptions.teenDriverAdditionBasis: Agent quote, $200/mo, to add Jordyn as a third driver to the EXISTING two-car policy. Charged once at household level, never to a listing.
costAssumptions.perCarInsuranceBasis: Real agent quotes by VIN and by model where we have them; otherwise a published fit on wheelbase (r=0.95) and, failing that, price. Each listing carries its own source and uncertainty. Horsepower was tested and does NOT predict premium here (r=0.05).
knownWeaknesses: Insurance is the single largest line item over six years. Real agent quotes now anchor it for five cars (matched by VIN, then by model); everything else is a fitted estimate whose error is published per listing rather than hidden. The teen-driver addition is NOT in these figures — it is a household cost, counted once in highlanderAndPlans.
Original MSRP, which drives the RTA MVET portion of registration, is estimated per model-year rather than looked up per VIN.
NHTSA complaint counts are not adjusted for sales volume, so raw counts are not comparable between a high-volume and a low-volume model.
Washington's used-EV sales-tax exemption appears to have lapsed 2025-07-31 and is deliberately NOT modelled.

kateResearch.label: Jaguar I-PACE

openRecalls.remedy: This is a placeholder campaign for the permanent remedy, which is stillunder development. This information will be updated when this activity is completed.

As an interim repair, the vehicles will have software installed to restrict the maximum state of charge to 90% whilst a permanent remedy is developed.

In line with recommendations made by manufacturers whohave had similar issues and until such time as the interim remedy has been completed, JLR request that customers take the following precautionsto minimise the thermal overload which can lead to vehicle fire:

• Only charge their vehicle to a maximum of 90% state of charge
•Park away from structures
• Charge outside

Customers can monitor the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App or inside the vehicle and should seek to physically stop the charging by unplugging the cable before a 90% state of charge is exceeded.

There will be no charge to the owners for this interim repair.

At your visit, your preferred Jaguar retailer/authorized repairer willprovide an update to the Battery Energy Control Module (BECM) software that will monitor the High Voltage (HV) battery operational status. Thiswill provide indication in the event the HV battery exhibits conditionswhich may lead to thermal overload condition.This software provides anenhanced level of driver warnings in relation to HV battery condition and in the event the software determines a risk exists, the HV battery charging capacity is limited to up to 75%.If this happens, the vehicle will prompt you to visit a Jaguar retailer/authorized repairer. Your retailer will inspect, and if necessary replace the affected HV battery module/assembly at no cost to you.Some vehicles also provide a Charging Limit feature that can be used by customers to limit the charge level. Customers may, until the recall is completed, set the charge limit to 75%.Instructions of how to limit the charging limit can be found in the Jaguar I-PACE Owner’s Manual in the Vehicle Preconditioning – Charging Limits section at www.ownerinfo.jaguar.com.Customers can also monitor and control the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App and stop charging when it reaches 75% state of charge.There will be no charge to the owners for this repair.

openRecalls.remedy: This is a placeholder campaign for the permanent remedy, which is stillunder development. This information will be updated when this activity is completed.

As an interim repair, the vehicles will have software installed to restrict the maximum state of charge to 90% whilst a permanent remedy is developed.

In line with recommendations made by manufacturers whohave had similar issues and until such time as the interim remedy has been completed, JLR request that customers take the following precautionsto minimise the thermal overload which can lead to vehicle fire:

• Only charge their vehicle to a maximum of 90% state of charge
•Park away from structures
• Charge outside

Customers can monitor the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App or inside the vehicle and should seek to physically stop the charging by unplugging the cable before a 90% state of charge is exceeded.

There will be no charge to the owners for this interim repair.

openRecalls.remedy: This is a placeholder campaign for the permanent remedy, which is stillunder development. This information will be updated when this activity is completed.

As an interim repair, the vehicles will have software installed to restrict the maximum state of charge to 90% whilst a permanent remedy is developed.

In line with recommendations made by manufacturers whohave had similar issues and until such time as the interim remedy has been completed, JLR request that customers take the following precautionsto minimise the thermal overload which can lead to vehicle fire:

• Only charge their vehicle to a maximum of 90% state of charge
•Park away from structures
• Charge outside

Customers can monitor the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App or inside the vehicle and should seek to physically stop the charging by unplugging the cable before a 90% state of charge is exceeded.

There will be no charge to the owners for this interim repair.

openRecalls.remedy: This is a placeholder campaign for the permanent remedy, which is stillunder development. This information will be updated when this activity is completed.

As an interim repair, the vehicles will have software installed to restrict the maximum state of charge to 90% whilst a permanent remedy is developed.

In line with recommendations made by manufacturers whohave had similar issues and until such time as the interim remedy has been completed, JLR request that customers take the following precautionsto minimise the thermal overload which can lead to vehicle fire:

• Only charge their vehicle to a maximum of 90% state of charge
•Park away from structures
• Charge outside

Customers can monitor the charging of their vehicle with the latest version of the Jaguar Remote App or inside the vehicle and should seek to physically stop the charging by unplugging the cable before a 90% state of charge is exceeded.

There will be no charge to the owners for this interim repair.
